scorecard.name: Workers using generative AI at work
scorecard.detail: Share of employed adults who used generative AI for work, St. Louis Fed survey, Jul 2026. Highest in computer and math jobs (69%) and management (63%); lower in office support (37%) and transportation (24%). Users say it saves about 2.1% of all work hours.

trend.text: Average of the last two readings: 42.9%, up from 36.2% a year earlier

scorecard.name: Tech investment relative to payroll
scorecard.detail: Business spending on computers, related equipment and software as a share of total employee pay, Q3 2026. Before 2023 it never topped 8.1%. Firms are putting more money into machines and code relative to people, which is what you'd expect if they are substituting one for the other.

trend.text: Latest: 10.7%, up from 9.0% a year earlier

scorecard.name: Tech equipment investment (inflation-adjusted)
scorecard.detail: Real spending on computers and related equipment over the past year to Q3 2026. Imports of computers rose 62%, so much of it is built abroad. More machines can lift output per hour without any efficiency gain.

trend.text: Growth over the past year: 29.1%, up from 20.8% a year earlier

scorecard.group: Work: are jobs and pay shifting?
scorecard.name: Young graduates' job-finding edge
scorecard.detail: Unemployment of college graduates aged 20–24 minus all 20–24-year-olds, 12-month averages to Sep 2026: 6.7% vs 7.4%. In 2002–19 graduates were always better off, by 1.4 to 6.8 points. Entry-level office work is what AI does best, so this is where many economists expect the first effects. The edge is now the smallest on record since 2002.

trend.text: Latest: -0.7 pts, up from -1.4 pts a year earlier

scorecard.group: Work: are jobs and pay shifting?
scorecard.name: Jobs in computer systems design
scorecard.detail: Change since Dec 2023, to Sep 2026, against +1.5% for all private jobs. Information jobs: -7.6%. Its gap with all private jobs (-5.3 points) is worse than all but 11% of same-length stretches in 2002–19; the worst, -14.5, came after the dot-com bust. Tech hiring also slumped in 2023 as interest rates rose, before most firms used AI.

trend.text: Gap vs all private jobs: -5.3 pts, up from -6.1 pts a year earlier

scorecard.group: Work: are jobs and pay shifting?
scorecard.name: Managers' pay premium over office staff
scorecard.detail: Change since late 2023 in managers' median weekly pay relative to office and administrative support workers, to Q3 2026. One theory (Imas, Koh and Legg, 2026) predicts the people who coordinate work gain while routine specialists lose. So far office pay has grown faster (4.1% a year vs 3.8%), the opposite.

scorecard.name: Output per hour, nonfarm business
scorecard.detail: Since the end of 2023, against 1.6% in 2004–19. Given how noisy quarterly data are, chance alone would produce a gap this large about 10% of the time; a reliable signal needs 5% or less.

trend.text: Growth over the past year: 2.1%, down from 2.7% a year earlier

scorecard.name: Output per hour, nonfinancial corporations
scorecard.detail: Since the end of 2023, against 1.4% in 2004–19. Given how noisy quarterly data are, chance alone would produce a gap this large about 18% of the time; a reliable signal needs 5% or less. This measure leaves out the self-employed and the harder-to-measure parts of the economy.

trend.text: Growth over the past year: 3.6%, up from 2.2% a year earlier

scorecard.name: Income-side check
scorecard.detail: Real income (GDI) minus real output (GDP) growth. GDI has grown 2.7% a year since end-2023, against 2.4% for GDP, through Q2 2026. Income is keeping pace, so output isn't obviously overstated.

scorecard.name: Underlying efficiency (SF Fed)
scorecard.detail: Since end-2023, after removing more machines, more skills and working harder (average of the SF Fed's quarterly figures). It grew about 2.1% a year in the 1997–2003 boom.

scorecard.name: Official TFP (BLS, annual)
scorecard.detail: 2023–2025, against 0.7% in 2004–19 and 1.5% in 1997–2003. No adjustment for working harder, so it overstates efficiency in a hot economy.

trend.text: Growth in 2025: 0.8%, down from 1.5% a year earlier

scorecard.name: Working harder (factory hours)
scorecard.detail: Weekly hours of factory production workers, Sep 2026, against 40.8 two years earlier (2018 peak 42.4). Longer weeks suggest extra effort and machine time are flattering the numbers.

trend.text: Latest: 42.0 hrs, up from 41.0 hrs a year earlier

scorecard.name: AI users vs hands-on industries
scorecard.detail: How much more professional & business services sped up than retail, leisure and construction, each measured against its own 2010–19 pace. 6% of 2010–19 stretches showed a gap at least as large, and dropping any one hands-on industry leaves +1.1 pts. To count, the gap must beat every 2010–19 stretch and stay above 1 point when any one hands-on industry is dropped.

trend.text: Gap: 1.8 pts, up from 0.3 pts a year earlier

scorecard.name: AI producers: information
scorecard.detail: Speed-up in output per hour since end-2023 against its own 2010–19 pace, bigger than in any 2010–19 stretch (max +2.8). This industry includes data centers and software publishers, which build and sell AI, so it shows AI production rather than use.

scorecard.name: Workers' share of business income
scorecard.detail: Change in labor's share of nonfarm business income since the end of 2023, against -0.4% a year in 2004–19. It is at its lowest since at least 1947. Chance alone would produce a decline this fast about 35% of the time. If machines substitute for people, more of the gains go to owners of capital.

scorecard.name: New businesses likely to hire
scorecard.detail: High-propensity business applications, 12-month average to Sep 2026, against 155k at the end of 2023 and 110k in 2019. A wave of lean AI-native startups would show up here.

scorecard.name: Inflation-adjusted interest rates
scorecard.detail: 10-year TIPS yield on 2026-11-04. Markets tend to push this up when they expect faster growth, but deficits and Fed policy move it too. In the late-1990s boom it was about 3.5–4.5% (Klein's estimate).

trend.text: Oct 2026 average: 2.8%, up from 1.8% a year earlier
